detail.longDescription: It’s been four weeks since I started learning Linux at Akwannya Hub, and I’m gradually building a better understanding of how Linux systems work beyond basic commands. This week, I explored four important areas: Bash scripting, computer hardware, the Linux filesystem, and network configuration. Here are some of the key things I learned. 1. Getting Started with Bash Scripting Bash scripting allows us to combine commands into a file that can execute a series of tasks automatically. A Bash script typically begins with a shebang: # !/bin/bash After creating a script, we can make it executable using: chmod +x script.sh ./script.sh I also learned about variables, user input, command substitution, conditional statements, loops, and exit codes. For example, a simple conditional statement: # !/bin/bash read -p "Enter your age: " age if [ "$age" -ge 18 ]; then echo "You are an adult." else echo "You are under 18." fi Bash scripting provides a way to automate repetitive tasks and build more efficient workflows. 2. Understanding Computer Hardware Another area I explored was the hardware that makes a computer work. Some of the key topics included: CPU: Processor architecture, including 32-bit, 64-bit, and ARM, as well as multicore processors and simultaneous multithreading. Memory: RAM and swap space, which play different roles in system memory management. Storage: HDDs, SSDs, and NVMe storage. Motherboards and buses: Technologies such as PCIe and USB. Power and firmware: Power supply units, UPS devices, BIOS, and UEFI. Linux provides commands that help us inspect hardware information: lscpu free -h lsblk lspci lsusb These commands make it easier to understand a machine's processor, memory usage, storage devices, and connected hardware. 3. Understanding Where Data Is Stored I also explored how Linux organizes files and directories according to the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS). Some important directories include: /home — users' personal directories. /bin and /usr/bin — locations for essential and other user commands. /sbin — system administration commands. /etc — system configuration files. /var — variable data, including logs. /lib and /usr/lib — locations for system libraries. I also learned how the PATH environment variable helps the shell locate executable commands. To investigate where a package has installed its files, different Linux distributions provide commands such as: dpkg -L package-name rpm -ql package-name Understanding the filesystem makes it easier to navigate a Linux system and locate applications, configurations, libraries, and logs. 4. Exploring Network Configuration Networking was another important part of this week's learning. I explored IP addresses, subnet masks, default gateways, network interfaces, DNS, ports, and SSH. Some useful commands include: ip addr ip link ip route ping example.com For DNS troubleshooting, commands such as these can help: host example.com dig example.com nslookup example.com I also learned about checking network connections and listening ports with ss : ss -tuln SSH allows us to connect securely to remote machines: ssh username@hostname_or_ip An important lesson was understanding SSH host key fingerprints and the known_hosts file. If a host's identification changes unexpectedly, it should be investigated rather than ignored. Final Thoughts Week four helped me connect several important pieces of the Linux environment: how scripts automate tasks, how hardware resources are inspected, how files are organized, and how systems communicate over a network. I'm beginning to see how these concepts fit together and why they matter for system administration, cloud computing, and software engineering. There is still a lot to learn, but every week gives me another opportunity to build on what I already know. Four weeks down.
